reader_summary: I can follow this section's question: whether more answer-time computation produces enough improvement to justify its full cost. In the planned example, one 80-token answer needs five verification tokens, giving 85; four 20-token answers need 20 verification tokens, giving 100. Holding model weights fixed does not hold the answering procedure or its cost fixed. For a comparison I would set an explicit budget and measure final accuracy, candidate-set coverage, selection failures, and actual expense. The cited 24-question table totals generation tokens and per-question batched-generation time; it now makes clear that the generated end-of-sequence marker EOS counts too. I can distinguish these generation-only times from complete request latency and the separately cited training/evaluation/saving cost. The example cannot predict any of those real durations or prove an equal-budget quality optimum.

examples.details: The two artificial totals follow from multiplication and addition: 1*80+1*5=85, versus 4*20+4*5=100. In the earlier-model table, each row aggregates 24 questions; k is the number of candidates for each question. Short answers allow up to 8 newly generated tokens each, while step answers allow up to 48, so the comparison does not hold total generation tokens equal. Step coverage improves 11/24 to 14/24 (three questions) at roughly eightfold token count (512 to 4,132), while majority answer accuracy improves 11/24 to 12/24. Lower short-answer elapsed time at larger k is explained as one batched run affected by execution conditions, so I would not turn it into a stable ranking. I understand which request stages the timing omits, and why the separate 45.71-second training/evaluation/save figure is a different cost. I have not independently verified or replicated these cited measurements.
